summary: Defines a backward-compatible extension giving IS-IS a three-way handshake when forming adjacencies on point-to-point links. Base IS-IS assumed the link layer was reliable and skipped this. The extension makes adjacency formation safer and still interoperates with systems that do not implement it. It replaced RFC 3373.

eli5.summary: Before two people start talking, it helps to say hello, hear hello back, and then confirm. This adds that extra confirmation step for routers, so both are sure the other can hear them.

questions: why is a three way handshake needed in is-is
what is the is-is three-way handshake
why does is-is need a three-way handshake on point-to-point links
subtitle: An optional extra field in IS-IS hello packets that lets two routers confirm they can hear each other before declaring a point-to-point link up.

tldr.problem: IS-IS assumes point-to-point links are reliable and only uses a two-way handshake, so one-way failures, lost synchronization packets and re-wired links can go unnoticed.
tldr.mechanism: Each router adds a new hello option (type 240) that reports its own three-way state, a circuit ID and the neighbor's system ID and circuit ID, and only declares the adjacency Up once it knows the neighbor is hearing it.
tldr.outcome: The extension is backward compatible and is a Proposed Standard that replaces RFC 3373; it also allows robust operation of more than 256 point-to-point links on one router.

today: RFC 5303 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2008. It obsoletes RFC 3373, and it is a minor edit of that document intended to advance it from Informational to Standards Track. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Two-Way Is Not Enough
sections.content:
The IS-IS routing protocol relies on ISO 10589 requirements for point-to-point links, so it provides only a two-way handshake when forming an adjacency. Each side declares the other reachable once it hears a Hello packet from it, then sends a Complete Sequence Number PDU (CSNP) to start database synchronization. If the link layer does not meet those requirements, the protocol does not operate correctly.

The RFC names three known failure modes. First, if the link comes back up (or a system restarts) and the CSNP is lost, the link state databases on both sides may stay unsynchronized for a full LSP refresh period, up to 18 hours. Second, if a link fails in only one direction, only one system notices; with two parallel links between the same systems, the system that missed the failure may keep sending traffic down the broken direction. Third, on some physical layers the far end can change without a link-down event, so a system may think it is adjacent to one neighbor when it is really adjacent to a third system.
sections.eli5: Two kids on walkie-talkies each hear the other say hello, but one kid's speaker is broken and never says so. Without a check, one of them keeps talking to nobody.

sections.title: The Three-Way State
sections.content:
The extension is optional and lets each system report its adjacency three-way state in its IS-IS Hello (IIH) packets. A system only declares an adjacency up when it knows the other side is receiving its hellos. There are three states:

  • Down: the initial state; no IIH with the three-way option has been received on this circuit.
  • Initializing: an IIH with the option has arrived, but the system does not know whether the neighbor is receiving its own IIH.
  • Up: the system knows the neighbor is receiving its IIH packets.

This three-way state is not the same as the adjacency state defined in ISO 10589. An adjacency may have both. For example, receiving an ISH moves the ISO 10589 adjacency to Initializing but leaves the three-way state Down until an IIH carrying the option arrives.

The neighbor's system ID and a new extended circuit ID are also reported, so a system can detect the same stream being received by several systems, only one of which can talk back.
sections.eli5: Each router holds up a card saying Not Yet, I Heard You, or We Both Hear Each Other. Only when the card says the last one do they start working together.

sections.title: Design Choices and Compatibility
sections.content:
The mechanism is similar to one in the Netware Link Services Protocol (NLSP), a variant of IS-IS for IPX traffic. NLSP uses two reserved bits in the IIH header. This RFC instead adds a separate option, because relying on reserved bits, although it should be backward compatible in theory, was felt to be risky. New option codes had been shown to work, as the deployment of Integrated IS-IS for IP (RFC 1195) did exactly this.

The new mechanism only comes into play when the remote system includes the option. If it is absent, the neighbor is assumed not to support it and the old procedures are used. A system that does not understand the option must ignore it and must not include it in its own IIH packets.
sections.eli5: Instead of scribbling in a margin that older readers might trip over, the routers add a new line to the note. Anyone who cannot read the new line just skips it.

sections.title: The Point-to-Point Three-Way Adjacency Option
sections.content:
The new IS-IS option is called Point-to-Point Three-Way Adjacency. Its type is 0xF0 (decimal 240) and its value is 1 to 17 octets long, made of four fields:

  • Adjacency Three-Way State (1 octet): 0 is Up, 1 is Initializing, 2 is Down.
  • Extended Local Circuit ID (4 octets): a unique ID assigned to the circuit when this system creates it.
  • Neighbor System ID (ID Length octets): the neighbor's system ID, if known. Its length equals the ID Length of the IIH PDU.
  • Neighbor Extended Local Circuit ID (4 octets): the circuit ID at the other end, if known.

A system supporting the mechanism SHALL include the option in its point-to-point IIH packets and MUST include the state field. The other fields SHOULD be included as the procedures describe.
sections.eli5: It is a small form with four boxes: my status, my line number, your name, and your line number. The status box is always filled in; the others only when known.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Hellos
sections.content:
When sending a point-to-point IIH, the system SHALL include the option and report its current three-way state, or Down if no adjacency exists. The Extended Local Circuit ID SHALL be unique among all circuits of that system, and it need not be related to the Local Circuit ID in the IIH. If the neighbor's system ID and circuit ID are known (state Initializing or Up), they SHALL be reported too.

On receiving an IIH, the rules are:

  • No option: the link is assumed to work in both directions and the ordinary ISO 10589 procedures apply.
  • Option with an invalid state: the PDU SHALL be discarded.
  • Neighbor System ID or Neighbor Extended Local Circuit ID present but not matching the local system: the PDU SHALL be discarded.
  • Otherwise the normal procedures apply, except that a new adjacency is created with three-way state Down and the table below decides what happens next.

This also protects against a link being moved to another interface that has the same local circuit ID: the PDUs are ignored and the existing adjacency fails.
sections.eli5: When a hello arrives, a router checks it names the right person on the right line. If the name or line is wrong, it throws the note away.

sections.title: The Adjacency Three-Way State Table
sections.content:
The action taken depends on the current three-way state of the adjacency and the state received in the neighbor's option:

Current stateReceived DownReceived InitializingReceived Up
DownInitializeUpDown
InitializingInitializeUpUp
UpInitializeAcceptAccept

A new action of Down raises an adjacencyStateChange(Down) event with the reason "Neighbor restarted" and the adjacency SHALL be deleted. Initialize raises no event and sets the three-way state to Initializing. Up raises an adjacencyStateChange(Up) event. The procedure still works if neither optional field is ever included, which gives compatibility with an earlier version of the option.
sections.eli5: Both sides keep saying how much they hear. Only when each one has heard the other say I can hear you do they both agree the line is open.

sections.title: More Than 256 Interfaces
sections.content:
IS-IS has an implicit limit of 256 interfaces because of the eight-bit Circuit ID field. In practice the limit really applies only to LAN interfaces where a system is Designated IS, since the circuit ID is only advertised in LSPs as part of the pseudo-node LSP ID. Point-to-point circuit IDs appear only in IIH PDUs and are used to detect a change of identity at the far end.

Implementers had supported more than 256 point-to-point interfaces by sending the same circuit ID on several interfaces. That weakens change detection, because links could be switched between interfaces without being noticed. Since the circuit ID is part of the new handshake, the 4-octet Extended Local Circuit ID gives a backward-compatible, larger number space.
sections.eli5: Old name tags only had room for 256 numbers, so some routers reused tags. Bigger name tags mean every line gets its own number.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The RFC says it raises no new security issues for IS-IS, and that IS-IS security may be used to secure the messages it describes, pointing to RFC 5304. For IANA, it specifies IS-IS Option 240 (0xF0), which had already been allocated; the RFC cites RFC 3359 for that allocation.
sections.eli5: The new note adds no new way to be tricked, and the existing locks for IS-IS messages can protect it too.
